Leslie Ironside

Leslie Ironside

Leslie Ironside  

Clinical commentary by Dr Leslie Ironside – consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist working in private practice in Brighton

Wisdom or oblivion – take your choice. From that warfare there is no release.W.R. Bion (1979)

I read the notes with great interest and empathy for both the therapist and patient. It is, however, a relevant, but strangely anonymous, experience to be writing without knowing more about the therapist. Is the therapist male or female, or, given the later material of the session what is the age of the therapist? Where does s/he come from? Where does s/he work? What is his/her professional background? To which school of thought does s/he/ belong? Fittingly, in terms of the family story, the refugee comes to mind; what do I really know about this person, who am I to comment on their work, how much do I understand them, what will they feel about my comments? Will I inadvertently tread on their toes? All also very relevant issues to the material presented. How though do I, how does the therapist, manage this gap in knowledge and understanding? How do I communicate in this commentary? How does the therapist communicate? Will I be experienced as a wolf diving in with the intention to devour? Is the therapist experienced in this way by the patient? My inner panic needs to be gathered safely in, to paraphrase Leonard Cohen.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Anne Hurley and Teresa Bailey

Teresa Bailey

Teresa Bailey  

We are pleased to present this issue of the Journal, which contains a variety of articles that reflect the clinical and research interests of child psychotherapists as well as the diverse settings in which we work.

The first three articles are themed around the topic of working with adolescents who are presenting with high risk of self-harm, suicide and other dangerous behaviour. The leading article by Janet Shaw uses Betty Joseph's concept of ‘addiction to near death’ to describe the treatment of an adolescent girl who has had to resort to a sado-masochistic way of relating in order to retreat from adult genital sexuality. The paper shows the link between the growing strength of sadism and masochism in adolescence and its contribution to the high risk and destructive behaviour seen in more disturbed adolescents. The clinical material is rich and fascinating, as we follow the therapist's attempts to manage the girl's and her own powerful aggressive feelings. The author's capacity to hold on to hope for the girl is remarkable in the face of her patient's denigrating, dismissive despair.

The next two articles also concern work with highly troubled adolescents. Anderson and her co-authors describe a qualitative psychoanalytic clinical research project about young people who had harmed themselves and/or attempted suicide. On a similar subject, Witkon's article describes the struggle to engage adolescents presenting significant risk and on the brink of the care system. The article by Anderson and her colleagues is helpful, timely and very pertinent. Her research team of seven experienced child psychotherapists used Grounded Theory to analyse the qualitative data that emerged from their work. This analysis led to the formulation of a theory they have named Truth Danger. The findings of the study are intriguing and helpful, as the theory allowed the researchers to identify not only explanations for suicidal behaviour, but more importantly, predictions for such behaviour. This has implications for us as clinicians working with this group of worrying and very troubled young people and their families, especially given the pressures on psychotherapy to maintain its central role in the treatment of suicidal young people.

A model of intervention at a psychoanalytic parent/child drop-in group in a poor district of Lima, Peru

Joshua Holmes

Joshua Holmes

12 Maresfield Gardens
London, NW3 5SU
UK

Joshua Holmes  

parent–child therapy, individuality, positive connotation, reflexivity, mentalisation, internal clinician, community psychoanalysis, alpha-function

The psychoanalytically informed work of a team of workers at a drop-in centre for families in a poor district of Lima is described. Interventions involve: accepting, connecting, playing and empowering. Clinical vignettes are used to illustrate the ways in which these interventions aim to help families. The acceptance of difficult feelings provides containment for attendees; acceptance of individuality fosters a greater capacity to mentalise. In viewing the patient as the relation between parents and child, connections are forged and encouraged between family members. Questions and difficulties that parents express are relayed to children in a palatable way, modelling the inclusion of children in the family dialogue. Playing is advocated and encouraged and elements of the fluid ‘frame’ impact on how playful interactions are shaped. Empowering takes place through encouraging reflexivity and dissolving fantasies of passivity. Questions about child behaviour are reflected back to the questioner or to other attendees, and pathologising diagnostic terms, if raised by families, are challenged and investigated, rather than accepted, encouraging families to carry on thinking. The implications of this model of work are discussed.

Author biographies

Janet Anderson (D.Psych.Psych.) is a Tavistock-trained consultant child and adolescent psychotherapist. She had a leading role for research in the North Essex Partnership NHS Foundation Trust. She is Chair of the ACP Research Committee and has published papers on research and is a co-editor of Child Psychotherapy and Research: New Approaches, Emerging Findings (2009).

Harriet Calvert is a child psychotherapist and adult psychoanalyst. She works for Windsor and Maidenhead CAMHS and she is also in private practice in Iver, Buckinghamshire.

Francesca Calvocoressi is the organising tutor for the SIHR Child Psychotherapy Training based in Edinburgh. She works part time in an NHS CAMHS multi-disciplinary team and offers regular consultancy to a residential school for primary aged children.

Elisabeth Kuhn Deakin is a psychologist with a Ph.D. in Psychology, Treatment and Intervention from Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio Grande do Sul (PUCRS), Southern Brazil. She is a psychotherapist at the Institute for Child and Family Health, Miami, Florida, USA.

Marina Bento Gastaud is a psychologist and Ph.D. student at Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), Southern Brazil. She is a researcher at Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio Grande do Sul (PUCRS), Southern Brazil.

Carolyn Hart is a child and adolescent psychotherapist working in a specialist CAMH service for vulnerable children in Sheffield. She has a particular interest in developmental trauma and the contribution of neuroscience to the field. Efforts at integrating findings from neuroscience into her clinical work have sparked her interest in relational psychoanalysis.

Joshua Holmes is a Ph.D. student at the Centre for Psychoanalytic Studies, Essex. As an assistant research psychologist, he is involved in interviewing depressed young people and their parents about their experience of therapy for IMPACT-ME study. His research publications have examined the role of countertransference in qualitative interviews, the influence of attachment and geography in agoraphobia and the psycho-social aspects of eating in a psychoanalytic parent–toddler group.

‘Make sure you keep our house safe!’ Thematic analysis of a children's psychotherapy group

Akasha Devi and Edwin Fenn

Edwin Fenn

22 Approach Road
London, E2 9LY
UK

Edwin Fenn  

Practice-based evidence, paranoid–schizoid and depressive position, Bion's group theory, work group and basic assumption group, group and gang states of mind, goal-based assessment measure

This paper describes a systematic thematic analysis of one particular latency-aged children's group and includes a discussion about potentially helpful outcomes measures. The impetus for our small, practice-based qualitative research project came from the two papers by Reid (1999) and Canham (2002) about children's psychotherapy groups, particularly Canham's (2002) paper, ‘Group and gang states of mind’. Canham and Reid used Bion's theories of group functioning as the basis of their technique with children's groups. We felt that it would be an interesting follow-on from Reid and Canham's findings to explore in some detail the specific therapeutic factors involved in a shift from paranoid–schizoid to depressive functioning in group therapy. We hoped that this might give us some helpful clinical indications as to the circumstances in which group rather than individual psychotherapy and parallel parent work should be considered as the treatment of choice. The paper concentrates exclusively on group work with latency-aged children, therefore referring mainly to the limited number of papers published about psychoanalytic group therapy with this age group.

Research digest: parents and parenting

Measures for assessing parenting in research and practice

Marjorie Smith

Child and Adolescent Mental Health, Wiley Online, 2011, Volume 16 (3): 158–66

Concepts of parenting and their development are briefly reviewed, as well as the variety and scope of application of the term. Issues in relation to the assessment of parenting are discussed, and three questionnaire-type measures are reviewed – the HOME Inventories, the Parenting Stress Index, and the Parenting Daily Hassles Scale. It is concluded that while these measures have a utility, theoretical developments in concepts of parenting will increasingly require the use of assessments more sensitive to the interactive and dynamic aspects of parenting. It seems probable that these will be observational methods or semi-structured interviews, rather than questionnaires.

Parenting behaviours and children's development from infancy to early childhood: changes, continuities and contributions

Leslie Morrison Gutman & Leon Feinstein

Early Child Development and Care, 2010, Informa, Volume 180 (4): 535–56

This study investigated trajectories of parenting behaviours and children's development from infancy to early childhood, associations between parenting behaviours and children's development and how these associations vary according to socioeconomic indicators. Mothers and children were examined from an ongoing longitudinal study of families resident in the geographic area of Avon in the UK. Using growth curve modelling, four waves of data were examined when the children were 6–42 months old. Findings suggest that timing is an important factor in the relationship between parenting and children's development. The positive association between mother–child interactions and children's development was evident 12 months later, whereas engagement in outside activities had both concurrent and later positive associations with children's development. Maternal education was also highlighted as a significant moderator suggesting that interactive parenting may have a protective role for children whose mothers have lower education.

Graham Music

Graham Music

Graham Music  

The master and his emissary: the divided brain and the making of the Western world, by Iain McGilchrist, New Haven and London, Yale University Press, 2010, reprint 2012, 544 pp., £11.99 (paperback)

McGilchrist's book was published in 2010 but continues to gain plaudits and influence. It sets out an important thesis about the relationship between the left and right hemispheres of our brains, exploring how the balance between these is currently shifting and considering the implications of this. It also has important points to make to psychotherapists as, at least indirectly, it provides a challenge to particular forms of therapy, suggesting serious limitations with the evidence-based ‘protocol’ driven culture, with its reliance on certainty, clarity and known formulae, in which we increasingly find ourselves. McGilchrist's thesis is in fact a very wide ranging one, suggesting that the way in which contemporary lives are being lived is affecting how our very brains function, leading to greater reliance on rationality, logic, certainty and control at the expense of emotionality, intuition, empathy and curiosity. It ultimately fires a desperate warning shot, cautioning us that the world we are creating is a diminished one, lacking in emotionality, creativity and openness, where feeling is shallow, happiness hedonistic, relationships superficial; a dystopian world in which nature is feared, intuition distrusted and love suspected.

His thesis is of course not entirely new. We first learnt about the different functions of our two cerebral hemispheres when Roger Sperry introduced an experimental treatment for epilepsy in the 1960s, which entailed severing left and right hemispheres. This was successful in treating epilepsy but had other dramatic repercussions. One patient was found doing up her blouse with one hand while simultaneously attempting to undo it with the other; another shook his wife with his left hand while his right tried to come to her rescue (Funnell et al., 2007). We learnt in effect that the hemispheres can act as separate spheres of consciousness and that each hemisphere tends to specialise in particular tasks. In split-brained patients, it is possible to present objects to one or other side of the brain and with the knowledge that the hemispheres cannot communicate, we learn which hemisphere processes which kinds of experience. For example in such patients, mathematical questions were successfully answered when presented to the left hemisphere but the right hemisphere showed poor mathematical abilities. The right hemisphere fared much better in tasks to do with music or visual perception, for example recognising pictures, objects and personal landmarks.

The early years of life: psychoanalytical development theory according to Freud, Klein and Bion, by Gertraud Diem-Wille, London, Karnac, 2011, 276 pp., £22.99

In many ways this was an excellent book that at times moved me deeply. However, I also found myself often perplexed as to who would be the appropriate reader. In her preface, Margaret Rustin suggests that the author, Gertraud Diem-Wille, has written the book for a ‘wide audience of parents and others involved in bringing up children’ (p. ix). This prospective audience links with one of the implied aims of the book, which is to introduce those not ‘in the field’ to an idea of the ways in which psychoanalytic understanding can contribute to people's lives. In her preface to the English edition, Gertraud Diem-Wille explains why she has chosen to interweave observational and sessional material with theory.

The balance of examples from observed babies in ‘normal families’ and children in analysis is based on the conviction that the awareness of unconscious emotional patterns between parents and child can have a helpful liberating impact on people who work with children and parents.

This aim means at times she states views on what constitutes good parenting in a way that cannot help but be judgemental and that occasionally I found uncomfortable. However, the theory, drawing heavily on Freud, Klein and Bion is hardly that which, in my opinion the average parent, nursery worker or teacher would be able to connect to. Gertraud Diem-Wille also states in her introduction that the idea for the book arose out of lectures that she was giving to psychoanalytic candidates. Yet with that type of audience in mind I was unsure how much this book might seem rather too simplistic, too much of a relatively superficial introduction. I rather think that it is a book that, for its theoretical content, is likely to appeal to those who have an interest in psychoanalytic ideas, but are still at quite an early stage in their voyage of discovery.

Child psychotherapy dropout: an empirical research review

Elisabeth Deakin , Marina Gastaud and Maria Nunes

Maria Nunes

Porto Alegre, Brazil

Maria Nunes  

child psychotherapy, outcome studies, dropout, psychoanalytical psychotherapy

This study aims to discuss the most recent data about child psychotherapy dropout, especially child psychoanalytical psychotherapy. The authors also try to offer some possible alternatives to prevent such a phenomenon. The definition of ‘child psychotherapy dropout’ is extensively discussed. The goal has been to attempt to create a standardised definition for psychotherapy dropout, which could help therapists from different theoretical backgrounds classify the term in a more unified manner.

Psychosomatic symptoms, post-traumatic stress disorder, holes, going-on-being, trauma, refugee, asylum seeker, anthropology

This paper will look at work carried out with asylum-seeking families and children within a hospital paediatric setting, exploring theories that can help us to understand how highly traumatic experiences, emotionally and cognitively unprocessed, may become expressed bodily. The case examples will show how these shattered and dislocated patients experience a range of physical symptoms from symbolic conversion manifestations to foreclosure of unthinkable and terrorising experiences displaced into the body. In the latter cases, there are particularly powerful and intergenerational effects upon the family as a whole, as the family becomes organised around physical symptomatology that covers ‘holes’ created by the trauma in their sense of ‘going on being’ as both individuals and as a family. These families can become over invested or hypercathect the physical fragility of children born into this matrix of trauma. The aim of this paper will be to draw upon psychoanalytic ideas in relation to psychosomatic symptoms, including Freud, Winnicott and Joyce McDougall amongst others and to try and integrate these ideas to some extent with both neurobiological understanding of the bodily aspects of feeling and emotion, as well as important anthropological understanding of identity in a cultural context.

[[RunningHead]]

Clinical material

Background

A 10-year-old white British boy who I am calling Cameron has been coming for weekly individual psychotherapy for just over one year. Cameron is the youngest of four siblings, all removed from their birth family. The eldest two, a boy and a girl, are known to have been subject to extreme neglect, physical abuse and sexual abuse. Their home was described as chaotic and squalid. Cameron was removed at 10 months and it is not known what he was or was not subjected to, other than extreme neglect. He was placed with the next youngest child, Jessica, who has moderate learning difficulties, in a foster placement, which lasted for two and a half years, until an adoptive couple was found for them together.

Cameron's (and Jessica's) adoptive parents are a white British couple. Their mother works for an insurance company. Their father, an engineer, runs his own engineering firm. Both parents are deeply committed to their two children, wish to understand them better and are supportive of therapy. Jessica also attends once-weekly therapy and the parents attend regular parent work alongside. Their mother is very anxious about both children and often overwhelmed by their needs; their father is talkative and friendly, though can struggle with his temper.

Referral

Both children were referred to the clinic two years ago, having previously had a period of art therapy at their school. The children were initially seen at the clinic with their parents for family therapy, before being referred for individual psychotherapy. There was also some input from psychiatry. Though Cameron's difficulties were understood in relation to his earliest experiences, he was diagnosed with ADHD and prescribed medication. However, this was discontinued at his mother's request when Cameron reacted to the medication by becoming very tearful and depressed and struggled to function.

Cameron's hyperactivity, and sometimes hyper-vigilance, was one of his parents' concerns; the feeling that he was always on the move, never settled and very distractible. Earlier on, they had also been worried by what they perceived as the shallow nature of his attachment to them and his lack of emotional contact. At school he was struggling with maintaining friendships (being either very controlling of friends by, for example, leading groups and clubs he formed with membership cards, or very passive socially) and subject to angry outbursts, though this is reportedly improved. However, Cameron was, and can still be, quite aggressive towards his mother.

Caroline Hart  

‘I've been in this place too’, would perhaps summarise my initial response to this session. That pervasive sense of irritation, both of the patient and the therapist, feels deeply familiar. So much so, that one of my first reactions was relief that, ‘this time, it doesn't involve me’. Then of course it dawned on me, that having agreed to contribute towards the clinical commentary, I would in some small way, be involved. That realisation, like the session itself, felt quite overwhelming. On reflection, I believe my reaction must in part, be my recognition that the issues I hope to discuss, are my issues too.

On reading the context while also holding in mind what we know about neglect (Alvarez, 1992; Music, 2009 and others) I was anticipating a rather numb ‘undrawn’ child. I was therefore quite taken aback to encounter a very alive and intelligent, if confrontational child. This sense of surprise started me thinking about pre-conceptions and how they are, or are not met. I went on to ponder about aliveness versus deadness in the relationship and the distance between patient and therapist in the session. My thought process continued with questions about how the therapist gets drawn into an unconscious enactment in order to stay in control. I intend to (briefly) reflect on these themes in terms of the interplay of both the patient's and therapist's unformulated experience, which I believe contribute to a sense of rigidity in the session.

Paradoxically, in contrast to this rigidity, a sense of surprise is also present from the very beginning of the session – Cameron and his father have actually arrived on time. At this point in the narrative, I had just been informed about the difficulty of managing the sessions immediately before a two-week break. Consequently, my sense was that this surprise was not exactly a pleasant one.

Editorial

Anne Hurley and Teresa Bailey

Teresa Bailey

Teresa Bailey  

This year marks the 50th anniversary of the publication of W.R. Bion’s Learning from Experience. In recognition of the profound influence of Bion’s work, this issue is dedicated to a celebration of the breadth and endurance of some of his key ideas across psychoanalytic work with children, parents, groups and organisations.

The first two articles by Suzanne Maiello and Louise Emanuel deal with early experience and Bion’s concept of containment is prominent in both. Maeillo’s paper examines the possibility of proto-experiences of the prenatal child in the context of Bion’s model of container/contained. These include auditory, tactile and kinaesthetic levels of awareness of the child in the womb to its environment and to the mother’s voice. The author hypothesises that the physical experiences of the foetus could have an emotional and psychological counterpart in the development of memory and a proto-mental container. Maiello explores thumb-sucking in utero as a way of thinking about a part-object model of container/contained. Also included is the description of the play of a three-year-old child and how an introjected configuration of container/contained can enable the development of both identity and the capacity for symbolic thought. This theme is also central in Louise Emanuel’s article, which describes therapeutic work within an Under Fives Service. She considers two clinical examples, a bereaved couple who lost their baby at six weeks and a three-year-old girl suffering from severe constipation, to explore the process of defensive evasion of separation through concrete means towards a more symbolic form of functioning. Her clinical work most ably demonstrates how anxiety related to separation and loss can be contained through the transformative function of ‘reverie’.

The next two articles have Bion’s theory of thinking as a clinically helpful backdrop to complex and challenging clinical work with latency-aged children. Ricky Emanuel’s article is a fascinating account of his work with a psychotic child in a special education unit when he was training in the 1970s. Emanuel had clinical supervision from Dr Meltzer and he describes how this enabled him to begin to understand some of his patient’s puzzling communications and to help bring about some internal change for him. It is a powerful and moving account of a developing relationship with a boy whose mind is inaccessible initially until Meltzer is able to offer some ways into the child’s emotional state, informed in particular by Bion’s understanding of hallucinatory phenomena.

Clinical material

Background

David is a seven-year-old boy of Nigerian heritage living in foster care. When his mother was young, she was sent from Nigeria to live in the UK with extended family. It is understood she had an abusive home life and eventually left the care of her extended family, subsequently becoming estranged from them. David was the product of a brief relationship and no information is known about his father. David's mother suffers from mental health problems and had a psychotic breakdown at the time of his birth. She was hospitalised several times in his early years. During these periods, David was placed in a temporary foster placement and would then return to the care of his mother once she was home. Support was invested to help his mother to care for him; however, eventually it was concluded that due to her health difficulties she was unable to care for him sufficiently and provide him with the safety and stability he needed. In 2008 when David was six, he was removed permanently from her care.

David was placed in a foster home and continued to have regular contact with his mother. However, due to difficulties between him and another child of a similar age in the placement, David was moved to a new foster home. This time he was placed with his current carers, a white Irish couple living with their 21-year-old daughter. David is described as a loving child who gets very anxious when adults leave him. He has a history of bedwetting and soiling. He would often appear to be in a dreamworld and would get very distressed during any points of transition, such as ends of lessons, although he had lots of friends at school.

The long-term plan was for David to be found a permanent family, which would be a closer cultural match for him. A referral was made to his local CAMHS service for intensive psychotherapy to help him with his emotional and behavioural difficulties, in the hope that this would help to increase the chances of a permanent family being found for him. I met David for an appointment with his carers before beginning three-times-weekly individual work.

I enjoyed reading this session five months into David's psychotherapy. It begins with David's provocative and aggressive behaviour that threatens escalation towards a sense of catastrophe (or breakdown), a feeling that the therapist links to the straw house in the fairy tale of the Little Pigs. I would guess that this is a spiral of interaction that both David and his therapist know well. However, as the session progresses, something more playful and symbolic emerges as David reflects on his anxieties both about the reliability of the structures around him and the destructiveness of his anger.

My view of this clinical moment is filtered by my own experience working with a busy local authority adoption team where I am involved in assessing children like David. I am involved in discussions about placement needs (including the match) and in adoption support, usually through meeting parents. The dynamics observed in the early part of this session are not unusual, as the children's anxieties about close relationships can be played out in controlling, provocative and aggressive behaviour that can hook new parents into negative spirals. These children can be extremely vigilant, because of early trauma, but also through compromised executive functioning and they can be highly reactive, often misreading their new parent's tentative responses. The emotional impact of this behaviour and pattern of relationships can trigger primitive anxieties in the parents and in the professional network. David's description of two separate prisons aptly describes the way that both children and parents can find it hard to escape from these negative spirals.

For David, the idea of separate and parallel prisons may be a description of internal object relationships, possibly linked to his early experience with a mother who one can only guess may have been at times self-preoccupied and scary. I wanted to ask what it felt like to be with David in the early part of this session: under attack, perhaps, helpless and small, wondering what might happen next. The therapist might have felt unhelpful or even abusive. It is difficult for therapists to retain a capacity to think under this sort of fire.

Sharon Estill Taylor

Journal of Loss and Trauma, Routledge, 2010, Volume 15 (5): 228–41

Asking the research question, ‘What is the lived experience of women whose fathers died in World War II?’ led to awareness of the unexplored impact of war loss on children. It was hypothesised that this research would show that women who experienced father-loss due to war would share commonality in certain areas. Areas of exploration including current demographic information; circumstances at the time of the father's death; data on the mother, father, stepfather, grandparents, and siblings; life perceptions; family relationships; romantic partnerships; and midlife experiences, were addressed in a heuristic interview process. Seven women were interviewed and they told their father-loss stories. Enquiry into the experience of childhood bereavement due to father loss is integrated into this study.

The path to posttraumatic growth versus posttraumatic stress disorder: contributions of event centrality and coping

Darnell Shuettler and Adriel Boals

Journal of Loss and Trauma, Routledge, 2011, Volume 16 (2): 180–94

This study examined positive and negative trauma outcome predictors within the same sample. Measures known to correlate with both posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms and posttraumatic growth (PTG) were included to replicate past findings, as well as additional measures minimally or not addressed in PTG research. Stepwise multiple regression analyses revealed PTSD symptoms were best predicted by visceral reactions to the event, event centrality, avoidant coping and a negative perspective of the event. In contrast, PTG was best predicted by event centrality, problem-focused coping, and a positive perspective of the event. These results are an important step to understanding differential paths to PTSD and PTG.

Simonetta M.G. Adamo is a child and adolescent psychotherapist, member of the Tavistock Society of Psychotherapists. Formerly Full Professor of Clinical Psychology at the University of Milan Bicocca, she has taught many courses based on the Tavistock model in Italy and co-organises the course ‘Working with disruptive adolescents’, held at the Tavistock Clinic. Her main areas of interest and research are infant and young child observation, psychotherapy of children with autistic disorders, counselling young people, psychoanalytically oriented work in paediatric wards, and the emotional aspects of teaching and learning relationships. She has published widely in international journals and has contributed to several books. She has also edited books on counselling young people, imaginary companions, and the psychodynamic approach to children with cancer. She has co-edited a book on work with disruptive adolescents with Gianna Williams.

Francesco Bisagni, a psychiatrist, was trained as a Jungian analyst in Italy. He completed his training as a child and adolescent psychoanalytic psychotherapist following the Tavistock model at the Associazione Italiana di Psicoterapia Psicoanalitica Infantile, of which he was a full member from 1998 until 2005. He is presently a member of the Society of Analytical Psychology and an affiliate member of the Association of Child Psychotherapists in the UK. He is also a member of the National Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis in the United States and a training analyst and supervisor at the Centre for Studies in Contemporary Psychoanalysis in Milan, Italy. He has taught for many years both in Italy and abroad and he has had works published in Italian as well as in international journals. He is in private practice as a psychoanalyst and child psychotherapist in Milan.

Leslie Ironside completed his training as a child and adolescent psychotherapist in 1989 and completed his doctorate, which focused on work with traumatised children, in 2001. Prior to this, he worked as a teacher with emotionally disturbed children. He was a consultant psychotherapist in the Health Service from 1994 to 2004. He also worked in private practice and developed the Centre for Emotional Development in Brighton, East Sussex. This centre aims to provide high quality educational conferences and lectures in the field of child and adolescent mental health and development. He now works as Director for the Centre and as a freelance practitioner and consultant. He has also developed a specialist interest in working within the field of fostering and adoption and the Centre is registered as Outstanding by Ofsted as an Adoption Support Agency. He has published a number of papers in this field.

Adoption, care system, consultation, container/contained, networks, psychic retreat, trauma

This article explores the process of consultation to professional networks, teams, groups and individuals concerned with the mental health of children and young people in the care system, and those adopted. Frequently there are significant elements of early trauma suffered by the young people and disruption in the professional organisation. The article describes the way in which clients’ narratives are brought together by, or impact upon the professional network around them. It then formulates a structural framework to assist thinking, often an early casualty when dealing with traumatic events. This is founded upon Bion's concept of container/ contained, Steiner's concept of ‘psychic retreats’ and Armstrong's application of this to organisations. The undermining of language so that it becomes unserviceable for emotional development is considered as the source of disruption of narrative thought. This necessitates the use of physical images, or models, as a basis for understanding.

Gail Phillips

Gail Phillips

50 Gloucester Drive

Gail Phillips  

The uninvited guest from the unremembered past: an exploration of the unconscious transmission of trauma across the generations, by Prophecy Coles, London, Karnac, 2011, 112 pp., £14.99, ISBN: 978 1 85575 700 4

In her most recent book, Prophecy Coles moves from the intra-generational world of sibling relationships to that of the trans-generational. She starts with some thoughts about the losses in Freud's life – beginning with the mourned loss of his daughter, Sophie, in 1919, and the death of her son, his grandson, two years later. These are deaths clearly remembered and written about by Freud. By contrast, she goes on to note some sibling deaths in Freud's family – not only that of his brother, but also that of his mother's younger brother – both named Julius. These deaths occurred within weeks of one another, when Freud himself was well under the age of two years. Coles muses about the echoes in Freud's thinking of these deaths, and their likely impact on his mother and, through her, on Freud himself, presumably a scarcely verbal toddler at the time of the losses.

Her interest in this book is to trace some of such echoes, as seen in literary characters and in her patients, back to their sources, often many generations before. She argues that the force of these aspects of the past, and their ability to unsettle, lies precisely in their being unremembered, unmarked. Uncovering them and making them available for thinking about can at least mitigate their force. That this would be important for individuals and their families is clear, and she acknowledges that her title links her work to Fraiberg's ‘Ghosts in the nursery' (1975). Fraiberg's ghosts are referred to as ‘the uninvited guests at the christening’: maybe a reminder of the story of Sleeping Beauty, underlining the power of such uninvited guests to disrupt and wreak havoc. The central chapters, focusing on particular individual ghosts, are framed by ones noting the wider ripples – family feuds, the holocaust and the trauma of war.

Lost for words: difficulty expressing feelings in work with three adolescent boys

Robert Tyminski

Robert Tyminski

3529 Sacramento Street
San Francisco, California
USA

Robert Tyminski  

Adolescent male development, alpha function, Anzieu, Bion, cutting, language problems, psychosis, skin ego, substance abuse

Case material of three adolescent boys is considered with regard to thematic similarity around acts of puncture. Their non-verbal communication is seen as a symptomatic acting out of an internal loss of containment. This resulted in psychotic disorganisation in which aspects of language appeared selectively impaired. Each boy struggled to express emotions and feelings, and was at a loss for words in attempting to describe how he felt. Anzieu's concept of the containing function of the skin ego is examined, as this is a useful idea for thinking about puncture of an internal shell, and what happens when it is not able to withstand disturbing internal forces. Bion's theory of alpha function is also explored to understand further a breakdown in emotional communication. Disruption of alpha function can result in bizarre images. In each case, disturbing imagery was a feature of therapeutic breakthrough, which followed incidents of puncture in the outer world. Various meanings of puncture as a clinical phenomenon are considered with regard to language, loss of an ability to express oneself, and the importance of images for regaining what might be regarded as a proto-form of alpha function as well as mending a torn skin ego.

Maria Pozzi-Monzo

Maria Pozzi-Monzo  

Neuropsychiatric disorders in children, genetic disorders, Attachment Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, Ritalin

This paper explores further the vast topic of child neuropsychiatric disorders – ADHD in particular. It refers to and expands on issues debated in an earlier paper ‘Ritalin for whom?’. In that paper, it was argued that those who benefitted most from children taking Ritalin were parents and teachers struggling with uncontained and out-of-control children under five, as well as doctors constrained by scarce resources and long waiting lists in NHS child services. This paper looks at the complex, inextricable and still somewhat mysterious interaction between genetic and environmental factors and what is meant by ‘genetic disorder’ when, for example, the diagnosis of autism, Asperger’s syndrome, ADHD is made. The author explores various avenues of research and focuses on the contribution of the psychological perspective offered by psychoanalytic thinking and attachment theory to understanding hyperactivity. This paper is mostly a review of theories, research and formulations, which help us explain some of the underlying factors in hyperactive children. Brief vignettes from infant observation, parent–infant psychotherapy and psychoanalytic treatment of children are used to support the main hypothesis that ADHD results from the interweaving of neuropsychological factors from birth onwards and can be treated by psychological interventions.

An application of Bion’s theory of thinking and transformations in hallucinosis. An experience of supervision with Dr Donald Meltzer

Ricky Emanuel

Ricky Emanuel

Pond Street
London, NW3 2QG
UK

Ricky Emanuel  

Child psychotherapy, psychotic children, hallucination, theory of thinking

I hope in this paper to show how Bion’s theory of thinking and his later theory of transformations in hallucinosis, enabled psychotherapy in a special school setting many years ago to be undertaken with a psychotic child who was constantly hallucinating. The work was carried out under the expert supervision of Dr Donald Meltzer who managed creatively to employ these theories to help me make sense of what seemed like incomprehensible communications. Bion’s theories were indispensable in being able to make sense of non-sense. I hope to illustrate the nature of hallucination where according to Bion, the sense organs operate in reverse: showing how the function of hallucination is to provide an alternative to thought about absent objects or ‘no-things’. The distinction between thought based on the capacity to bear the frustration about the absence of the ‘no-thing’ long enough to discover its meaning, is contrasted with the immediacy of hallucination where the ‘meaning’ is already ‘known’. The nature and function of naming is explored along with its precursor: the binding of phenomena. I also discuss how rare it is nowadays for child psychotherapists to treat children like this as they tend to be medicated and not referred for psychotherapy.

The paper describes the conclusive phase of the psychotherapy of a young man who suffered from Asperger's syndrome. The patient had been referred as an adolescent, at which time he was very isolated and spent most of his life in the company of countless imaginary friends that were quasi-delusional constructs. After several years of therapy, the patient was able to relinquish this fantasy world and his bizarre interests, and become involved and successful in his studies. His emotional development, however, was still stuck. Meltzer's theory of the aesthetic conflict and his ideas concerning the impasse at the threshold of thedepressive position contributed to throwing light on this phase of the psychotherapeutic process, and finally helped the patient to emerge from his upside-down world and begin to acknowledge the value and beauty of intimate relationships.

‘If I knew where the enemy, or even Germany was, we could have fired in that direction’: Bion's experience of war

Meira Likierman

Meira Likierman

Dean's House, 1 Sussex Place, Regents Park
London, NW1 4SA
UK

Meira Likierman  

Ypres, tank-crew, Cambrai, Dispatches, DSO, breakdown, fear, truth, transformation

During the First World War, Bion fought in three major battles over a period of two years. He left ample writings both honest and soul searching. Travelling to The Front under raging pressure from his father, he enlisted in a state of mind, which fluctuated wildly between wanting to be a ‘hero’ and sudden fears that made him join the Tank Corps under the illusion that in a tank he would be protected. While the tank was disappointing in this respect, it put him in charge of a crew, thus giving him the first glimpse of group processes. This article charts some of Bion's experiences of war, their emotional impact on him and the transformation he underwent. The origins of some of his later thinking can be glimpsed in some of the experiences he had at this critical time in his life.

It is strange to comment on an unknown person's work. Having looked at this a number of times, I find I enjoy and respect the therapist. To me this therapy is a going concern and both participants come alive in a convincing way.

So what am I doing adding my thoughts to it? Is it right to interfere? There is something quite precious about an ongoing piece of work, which is going well enough and indeed even more than well enough, and where my sense is of a therapist with a well working internal and perhaps external supervisor. Of course, the reality is that now the work has long continued and is somewhere else and we, the readers are in the privileged position of having been given an opportunity to glimpse into a therapy. We can use it as something to play with, a touchstone in our own minds. I find myself putting it alongside my own world of therapy experiences, current and past thoughts, ideas, memories, all interestingly jogged into life.

Harriet Calvert  

My first impression on reading this case was of the wealth of material. The richness of the description felt at times rather overwhelming. I wonder if this was also the experience of Karl. The second impression was of how closely my impressions of the session were confirmed by Karl's intervention. I did however feel that I have a few things to add.

The description of Cameron as laid out in the section ‘Referral’ seems to describe a fairly typical presentation of a child who has experienced serious neglect in his infancy. In fact, he reminds me of a patient of mine who like Cameron was removed from his birth mother in infancy. The features of hyper-vigilance, sometimes hyperactivity (often mistakenly labelled as simple ADHD), ‘shallow nature of attachment’ and ‘lack of emotional contact’ I have often seen in children with this kind of history. Furthermore, the aggression, the ‘loneliness deep inside’ and the lack of trust seem to me often to characterise these children.

I will now look at the session with this description of this child in mind. At the beginning, Cameron’s statement that “something stinks” tells of how he feels that the setting, maybe the whole therapy, had somehow changed, probably as a result of the break in therapy: the setting was felt to have gone bad. At the same time, he tells about his difficulties of holding his therapy in mind without it going bad. I think Cameron felt that the therapist had not protected the therapy and the setting enough. “It had gone mouldy”. This makes Cameron angry and he retaliates by spilling his water. This gradually produces a state of mind in Karl, of anger and irritation (projective identification). The task Cameron sets for Karl unconsciously is how to process these feelings of anger and irritation. I believe that these dynamics then continue to dominate this session, something that Karl soon became aware of.

The sequence early on in the session starting with Cameron telling Karl about his collectable rubber-edged discs and Cameron talking about disappointments, also contains some mention of Cameron becoming concerned about his earlier attack on the therapy when he momentarily became concerned about the water he had spilt and what it might do and whether Karl was angry with him.

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Anne Hurley and Teresa Bailey

Teresa Bailey

Teresa Bailey  

This is a general issue of the Journal although a theme connecting many of the articles is the dynamic interconnection between mind and body. This particularly comes into view when they are un-reconciled, as we know can be the case in situations of trauma, premature bereavement or interruption to early relationship as the articles presented here will confirm.

The first two articles take trauma as a central focus, which undoubtedly will be of interest to the readership. The first by Paddy Martin considers how unprocessed traumatic experience finds bodily expression and the following article by Francesco Bisagni highlights perceptual distortion in particular as a response to trauma.

Henry Maudsley was a physician working in the UK in the nineteenth century who addressed the Royal College of Physicians in London in 1870 with a lecture concerning body and mind and an inquiry into their connection and mutual influence. Maudsley lends the inspiration to the evocative title of Paddy Martin's original article, ‘Grief that has no vent in tears, makes other organs weep’. Martin draws on neuroscience and anthropology to complement his psychoanalytic exploration of psychosomatic illness. He describes clinical work in a hospital paediatric setting with asylum-seeking families who have survived horrific acts of war. The entrenched physical symptoms of his patients in the absence of organic cause and their wish for physical treatment is the backdrop to Martin's in-depth analysis of the many mechanisms underlying psychosomatic illness. What comes across strongly in his article is the complexity and entanglement of the physical and psychological as the slow and painful work of attaching meaning to both symptom and experience is struggled with in therapy.

The discord between experience and bodily reaction also features in Bisagni's article, which is a painful account of psychotherapy with a latency boy who discovered the body of his dead father following his suicide. The voice of the child, Fabrizio, is a powerful and moving one as he recounts the day he found his father hanging from a rope and the impossibility of making sense of what he encountered. The confusion, perceptual disorientation and sensory alteration of his experience is painfully conveyed in these traumatic circumstances. Bisagni's makes interesting theoretical connections with the damage to the contact barrier, and transitory psychotic disintegration in the face of overwhelming trauma. This theme is also present in the next article by Robert Tyminski, ‘Lost for words: difficulty expressing feeling in work with three adolescent boys'. In his description of clinical work with these patients, the inaccessibility of language to describe emotional content is linked to internal rupture of various kinds.

Prenatal experiences of containment in the light of Bion's model of container/contained

Suzanne Maiello

Suzanne Maiello

Via Dalmazia 16A, I-00198
Rome, Italy

Suzanne Maiello  

Prenatal shapes in space, prenatal thumb-sucking, miscarriage, dynamic relation between container and contained, theory of thinking, K and −K link

This paper explores the idea of possible proto-experiences of the prenatal child in the context of Bion's model of container/contained. The physical configuration of the embryo/foetus contained in the maternal uterus represents the starting point for an enquiry into the unborn child's possible experiences of its state of being contained in a container. The paper takes into consideration the sensory dimensions of auditory, tactile and kinaesthetic levels of awareness of the prenatal child in relation, respectively, to the maternal voice and the uterine environment. The author's hypothesis is that concrete prenatal experiences of containment may have their mental counterpart in the development of a proto-mental container and memory, the existence of which can be observed in the newborn infant. It is also suggested that prenatal proto-experiences of containment may prepare the child for further postnatal realisations of the pre-conception of containment and represent the experiential basis for the encounter with the breast. Observations of newborn babies in an obstetric ward, as well as the observation of a prematurely born child, seem to confirm the idea that the intrauterine experience of container/contained plays a role in the child's prenatal development. The meaning of prenatal thumb-sucking is explored in terms of the model of container/contained at a part-object level. An observation of the play of a three-year-old child offers material for further thought about the meaning and function of the introjected configuration of container/contained for the development of a sense of identity and symbolic thinking. The clinical case of an autistic child who survived a threatened miscarriage shows how the emotional containment in psychotherapy allowed the formerly inaccessible nameless dread to re-emerge and be represented and shared.

[[RunningHead]]

Understanding suicidal behaviour in young people referred to specialist CAMHS: a qualitative psychoanalytic clinical research project

Jan Anderson , Margaret Hurst , Ana Marques , David Millar , Sue Moya , Lesley Pover and Sue Stewart

Sue Stewart

UK

Sue Stewart  

Grounded Theory, Truth Danger Theory, hidden truth, fractured reality, risk, incongruent presentation

A qualitative psychoanalytic clinical research project using a post-Kleinian contemporary approach was undertaken by a team of seven qualified and experienced child psychotherapists working in community Tier 3 Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS). A number of referred young people who deliberately harmed themselves or attempted suicide, who fulfilled the inclusion criteria and consented to participate, were offered an extended individual and family assessment. Grounded Theory analysis of the qualitative data led to the formulation of the Truth Danger Theory. Typical situations in which suicidal behaviour occurred were identified, including intergenerational confusion, neglect, physical and/or sexual abuse within the family, Oedipal conflict, maternal depression and families in which there was a chronically ill sibling. We found that there was a marked disparity between the young person's experience of relationships in the family and the family's own account of their situation, a fractured reality. This can be reflected in an incongruence in the young person's presentation, which may be misleading when assessing risk. The young person feels him/herself to be in a dead end from which there seems to be no escape. Self-harm, for some, contains this impossible dilemma (albeit pathologically) but when it does not, suicide may seem the only option. The Truth Danger Theory provides explanations and predictions for suicidal behaviour and has implications for clinical practice.

[[RunningHead]]

Shrapnel: latency, mourning and the suicide of a parent

Francesco Bisagni

Francesco Bisagni


20129
Milan,
Italy

Francesco Bisagni  

Parental suicide, mourning, acute trauma, latency, archetype, preconceptions

The aim of this paper is to describe some acute responses to the suicide of a parent, through the account of the analytic psychotherapy of a latency child who found the body of his dead father. The acute traumatic responses of the child show that the perceptual apparatus, time and space are subverted, while the functioning of the contact barrier is deeply damaged. The importance of the environment in facilitating the first stages of the mourning process is stressed as well as the pre-traumatic personality structure. Both the Bionian model of preconception and the post-Jungian notion of archetype, revisited in terms of an unsaturated predisposition, are considered from a theoretical point of view. Preconceptions and archetypal dispositions to survive traumatic events are very important to the therapeutic outcome, along with the opportunity to start the treatment as early as possible after the traumatic event. This is particularly relevant in relation to the latency period, in terms of the capacity to contemplate the effects of the drives. The importance of allowing the child to work through all the stages of mourning is also considered, particularly rage, protest and hostile fantasies towards the lost object. The clinical material is structured as a narrative in an attempt to evoke the emotional climate experienced during the sessions as well as the state of mind of the child. The narrative is a secondary elaborated account with condensation and displacement at its core, like in dream work. Events, filtered through the analyst's state of self, are reported by lending the first person to the child in the narrative reconstruction.

Holding on; being held; letting go: the relevance of Bion's thinking for psychoanalytic work with parents, infants and children under five

Louise Emanuel

Louise Emanuel

120 Belsize Lane
London, NW3 5BA
UK

Louise Emanuel  

Containment, reverie, mourning, constipation, encopresis, bereavement, ‘second skin containment’, somatic

This paper attempts to convey how the ideas of Klein, Bion and Bick underpin psychoanalytically based interventions with parents, babies and young children in the Camden Under Fives' Service, Tavistock Clinic. As the title suggests, my focus is on ways in which anxiety relating to separation and loss, can be contained through the transformative function of ‘reverie’. I describe two clinical examples, of a bereaved couple who lost their baby at six weeks and of a three-year-old child suffering from severe constipation, to explore the role of therapeutic work in facilitating a shift away from a defensive ‘holding onto’ a concrete object as a means of evading separation, towards a more symbolic level of functioning, feeling ‘held in mind’. Steiner's description of the mourning process moving along a continuum from ‘fear of the loss of the object’ towards ‘experience of loss of the object’ as the patient shifts away from the ‘paranoid–schizoid’ towards a more ‘depressive position’ and the successful completion of mourning, is linked to Bion's concept of container-contained. The role of the clinician as ‘container’ of unprocessed states in young children, is discussed and linked to the recognition of ‘turning points’ in brief and longer-term work with under fives.

Kristen Carey

The authors discuss an application of Bion’s conceptualisation of thinking and non-thinking states (K and –K links) to the treatment of a nine-year-old girl. The authors consider Bion’s interrelated concepts such as K and –K, container/contained, maternal reverie, and the development of thinking through alpha function to be highly applicable to child treatment. The afore-mentioned conceptual elements are used to elucidate case material over two consecutive hours. A K link is established between therapist and patient, the fragility of which link is then demonstrated by its deterioration into a –K link. Complex issues about knowing and not knowing are central in this girl’s clinical presentation. She was conceived through in vitro fertilisation (IVF), and subsequently diagnosed with cerebral palsy. The authors consider the emotional impact of this origin story and how the parents relate to it. The authors discuss how parents sometimes cope with perceived losses by wishing to shield or protect their children. This can have repercussions for children’s efforts to know (K) and not to know (−K). The fear that emotional knowledge will be too painful to bear can interfere with ‘learning from experience’. Bion’s premise that the purpose of analysis is the growth of the mind is synonymous with the child analyst’s goal of fostering development and understanding impediments to development.

Yael Witkon

This paper describes the setting up and the first year of running of an innovative outreach service for adolescents on the edge of care that aimed at redressing family breakdown and preventing placements in the care system. It was a collaborative endeavour between social services and a child and adolescent mental health provision to facilitate the engagement of hard to reach young people and families that often presented high levels of risk. This article describes a distinctive model of applied psychoanalytic work with individuals, families and the networks of practitioners and agencies around the case. It focuses on the integration of two perspectives: the individual and the family on the one hand and the organisation on the other. Case examples illustrate how our psychoanalytic and developmental framework illuminated our understanding of frequently extreme acting out behaviour and parental difficulties in terms of underlying intergenerational trauma, which was often re-enacted. This framework also helped in understanding the difficulties that practitioners experienced and how these related to individual and family dynamics. The article describes the significance of containment in the treatment of adolescents and families in crisis as well as in supporting the professional network.

‘We should be playing, not talking’: play, self-agency and moving towards depressive moments

Margaret Poynton

Margaret Poynton

Cape Town, South Africa

Margaret Poynton  

projective identification, trauma, play selves, developmental object, psychic integration

This paper describes the use of play in the psychotherapy of a latency child from a severely traumatised background. It considers the meaning of play in relation to the role of the psychotherapist and to psychotherapeutic technique and explores its functions in terms of the child's development. The paper documents the psychotherapist's learning experience about the difficulty of trying to make the ‘right’ interpretations and her consequent realisation of the intrinsic value of play in psychotherapy. In considering these themes, the author explores how, by placing interpretation secondary to play, the therapy enabled the development of the child's creativity and self-agency, facilitating a movement from primarily paranoid–schizoid defences towards the beginnings of a depressive position.
